title: Terumah: the poles stay in (Exodus 25:15)
hook: the ark's carrying poles are never removed, always ready to travel

segments.voice: Yesterday, keruvim, the cherubim facing each other on the ark. Your line was the voice between the faces. Today, the last day of Terumah, and a small detail on the side of the ark.

Some people keep a go-bag by the door: a change of clothes, a phone charger, copies of important papers. Firefighters leave their boots standing inside their pants, ready to step into. New parents keep a hospital bag packed for weeks. Not because they expect to leave this minute, but because life moves, and they want to be ready when it does. The ark has rings on its sides, two on each side, and through them, two wooden poles covered in gold. Most furniture loses its handles once it's in place. Not this.
screen: `A GO-BAG BY THE DOOR.` → `BOOTS READY TO STEP INTO.` → `RINGS AND POLES ON THE ARK.`

segments.voice: The instruction, in the old Jewish translation: "The staves shall be in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it." Staves means the carrying poles, in Hebrew badim. Other pieces of the sanctuary have poles too, but for the ark the Torah says it outright: they stay in. Always. The Talmud treats this as a real commandment: pulling the poles out of the ark would break a prohibition. Why? The Torah doesn't say. Some said it was so no one would need to handle the holy ark directly when it moved. Others read a message in it. Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch, a German commentator, wrote that the poles show the Torah inside was never meant to be tied to one place. Wherever the people go, it goes with them. Later, when Solomon set the ark in the Temple in Jerusalem, the book of Kings says the poles were still in, so long their ends could be seen from the holy place. Even at rest, it was ready to travel. Later Jewish readers found that detail fitting. In exile, Jews carried the Torah to Babylon, to Spain, to Poland, to Yemen, to New York. The ark was gone, but the habit of readiness stayed. And with that, Terumah ends: willing hearts, among them, gold inside and out, the facing cherubim, and the poles that stay in.
screen: `THE STAVES SHALL BE IN THE RINGS.` · `THE TALMUD: NEVER REMOVE THEM.` · `HIRSCH: NOT TIED TO ONE PLACE.` · `STILL IN, EVEN IN THE TEMPLE.` · then, large: `READY TO TRAVEL.`

segments.voice: Suppose you had to move tomorrow, somewhere far. Not the furniture: name one or two things that make you who you are, a habit, a few words you live by, a practice from this path, a voice you'd keep in your head. Then ask whether each is ready to travel, or only works in one room, one routine.
Terumah. The portion we finish today, whose ark keeps its carrying poles in, always ready to travel with its people.
Your line: ready to travel. A week of laws and gifts: the widow, do then understand, willing hearts, the inside gold, the facing faces. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition counts the ban on removing the ark's poles among the Torah's commandments, and teachers often read it as a sign that Torah study and practice travel with Jews wherever they live.
